commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.

commands.name: doctor

Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

## What to build

werk starts each pipeline agent with a role in its environment. This ticket makes the same role pick the agent's model. One small pure table maps each role to a pinned model id and an optional advisor: the spec writer, the ticket writer and the grader run on Opus; the builder runs on Sonnet with Opus as advisor; every reviewer role, the held-out step author, the held-out binder and the overseer classifiers run on Sonnet. - [ ] No entry of the table uses a model alias.
- [ ] The chat agent's launch still uses the model chosen in the chat selector.
- [ ] The table is a pure module on the pure list and passes the coverage gate.

- `make test`
- `make test-coverage`
- `make typecheck`
- `make lint`

## What to build

Each project gets its pipeline log: one append-only file in werk's store, one event per line, tracked by git like the decision log. A pure fold reads it; nothing in v0 builds a report over it. Detail files sit beside it and are not tracked: one file per agent session holding its full stream, and one folder per plan holding its copy.

A plan is the first writer. When it starts, it appends a plan start event that lists every scope card with its tier and the log position of that card's last change, plus the size of the input: the card count per tier and the length in characters of the scope text in the prompt. Each writer step appends a step start, and on exit a step end with wall time, cost and the token breakdown (input, output, cache read, cache write), the result, and the name of its session file. When the plan ends, it copies the spec, every ticket it wrote or changed, and each writer's answer records into a folder of its own, lists the ids of the open tickets it kept unchanged, and appends a plan end event that names that folder and the result. A copy is a record only: no plan or build reads it.

The plan's board log events stay as they are. The pipeline log module and the session file writer are shared, so the builder loop, the merge loop and the held-out run later append to the same log through them.

- [ ] A scripted plan appends a start event whose scope list names each card with tier and log position, and the counts per tier.
- [ ] Each writer step has a start and an end with cost, tokens, wall time, result and a session file that exists beside the log.
- [ ] After a second plan of the same subtree, its copy folder holds only the changed spec and tickets and lists the kept ticket ids.
- [ ] The copy folder holds the answer records each writer returned.
- [ ] A comparison of two plan start events shows which scope card's log position changed between them.
- [ ] The session files and copy folders are ignored by git; the pipeline log is not.
- [ ] The pipeline log fold is a pure module that passes the coverage gate.

- `make test-coverage`

touches: build verb, builder loop, agent runner, pass prompt, check runner, pipeline log

## What to build

`werk build <ticket-id>` builds one ready ticket in the project's target repository. It makes a worktree branched from the main line's tip. Each pass starts a fresh agent with the role builder, on the model the role table names, whose prompt starts with `/implement` and holds the ticket, the spec lines of its stories, its cited cards with their rejected options and reasons, its checks, the index of decided cards with a rule to search the map before deciding what no cited card gives, and the last failure cut to about 4000 characters; the first pass is told nothing is done yet. No conversation passes between passes. After the agent exits, the loop commits what it left as pass n.

The loop then runs the ticket's checks in order, each a make target whose exit code is the verdict, stopping at the first red one. A red check runs once more on the same commit: green on the rerun records the cause flaky and the check counts as green; a crash, timeout or missing tool before the code ran records check infrastructure and is not rerun. A red pass feeds the next pass. The retry cap (default 5) counts passes across all builds of the ticket. Every time limit is a parameter, clamped by the shared budget.

A green build moves the ticket to merging and records its branch; a build red at the cap moves it back to ready with the reason. Board events record build started (naming the process and the session log), each pass, and build ended. Each agent's stream goes to its own session file beside the pipeline log. The pipeline log gets each pass and each check's start and end with wall time, cost, tokens, result, and for a red step its gate and cause, so effort per ticket can later be folded from it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A fake builder whose edit makes `make test` pass ends green in one pass and the ticket moves to merging with its branch.
- [ ] A fake whose checks stay red stops at the cap and the ticket goes back to ready with the reason.
- [ ] A check that fails then passes on rerun is recorded as flaky and does not cost a pass.
- [ ] The second pass's prompt holds the first pass's failure, and no conversation from it.
- [ ] The builder launch record shows the role builder and the model and advisor from the role table.
- [ ] The pipeline log holds a start and an end for every pass and check, with cost on agent steps and gate and cause on red ones.
- [ ] A build with no target repository set exits 1 and names the target operation.

## Checks

- `make test`
- `make test-coverage`
- `make typecheck`
- `make lint`

title: Every build opens a card obligation, and a pass closes it with a proposed card or with the cards it followed
cites: werk-loop

## What to build

When `werk build` starts, before any code is written, it appends a card obligation for that build to the decision log. The obligation is data, not a card: it is in no view of the map and in no rollup. Each pass's prompt names the obligation and tells the builder the two ways to close it: propose one card for each decision that no cited card and no searched card gives, or record that the pass made no new decision and name the decided cards its choices came from.

A pass that proposes a card closes the obligation with that card. `werk followed <obligation> --cards a,b` closes it with the record "no new decision" and the named cards, printing the obligation id and the cards; it is a fact in the log and needs no accept. A call without cards, a card that is a ghost, removed, unknown or not decided, an unknown obligation, or one already closed is refused with exit 1, names what is wrong, and writes nothing. An obligation that a build leaves open blocks nothing.

The fold exposes, per ticket, the cards its builds proposed (with proposal or accepted) and the cards a record followed, so the board's ticket drawer and the grader can read them.

## Acceptance criteria

title: An overseer inside each build pass cancels a stalled agent, answers its permission asks, and catches a loop
cites: lp-overseer
blocked_by: 30

touches: overseer, agent runner, overseer verdicts

## What to build

The overseer is plain code inside the runner that starts each build pass, grader, reviewer, step author and binder session; chat sessions get none. It asks the agent for partial messages and counts every streamed token as an event, without writing tokens to the session file. The silence clock starts at the agent's first event: no event for 60 seconds after that cancels the session, unless a tool call is in flight. For a call in flight, it reads the CPU time of the agent's child processes: growing CPU time means working; flat CPU for 60 seconds cancels it; a call with no process of its own cancels like silence. A probe that cannot read the process table counts as unknown, cancels nothing, and is logged. Only the wall-clock cap stops a session that never starts.

A builder's permission ask goes to a classifier agent with the role ask-classifier, on the model the role table names, with the tool, its input and the ticket; it allows or denies with a comment; no verdict means deny. Every 5 minutes, a classifier with the role loop-classifier gets the brief and the tool calls since its last verdict and says looping or not; no verdict means not looping, and it is skipped when no new call came. Looping cancels the session and the next pass gets the reason. A cancelled builder pass commits its edits, skips the checks, counts against the cap, and the next brief says why. A silent grader or reviewer fails as a step with silence as the reason. Every act is a line in the session file and the live log. All limits are parameters in milliseconds for tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A fake that prints one event then stalls is cancelled after the silence limit, and the next pass starts.
- [ ] A fake that is slow to start but then keeps printing is never cancelled for silence.
- [ ] A tool call whose process burns CPU past the limit is not cancelled; a flat one is.
- [ ] A failed process probe cancels nothing and is logged.
- [ ] A builder ask with a fake classifier that denies reaches the agent as a deny with the comment.
- [ ] A fake classifier answering looping cancels the pass and its reason appears in the next brief.
- [ ] The verdict logic is a pure module that passes the coverage gate.

- `make test`
- `make test-coverage`
- `make typecheck`
- `make lint`

## What to build

`werk run <subtree-id>` is the person's start of a run over that subtree's tickets; running it again resumes. Its first event in the board log is the tier, always feature, since v0 has no way to say or raise a tier, and every gate it reaches waits for a person. A run started event names the merge-loop process; a run ended event closes it. A start refuses while a run on the same subtree or an ancestor is in progress, and names that run.

The loop first merges any ticket already in merging, then builds ready tickets whose blockers are merged (one at a time in this ticket) through the full builder loop, and takes each finished ticket through a merge queue one at a time: it merges the ticket's branch onto the main line's tip in a detached temporary worktree and runs the ticket's checks there. Red checks merge nothing and send the ticket back to building with the failure; the next build starts from the old branch when it sits on top of the main line. Green moves the main line only from the value it had when the merge started; a checkout of the main line moves with it by fast-forward, and local changes that block the fast-forward stop the loop with nothing moved. The ticket goes to done. Each merge is a step in the pipeline log.

A ticket at its retry cap moves to blocked with the reason, with every ticket that needs it, and the loop goes on with the others; the run ends only when nothing can build or merge, and reports each stuck ticket and what waits on it. A loop that stops for any reason moves every ticket it left in building or merging back to ready with the stop reason. G2 belongs to the main line's tip and waits until every ticket of the subtree is merged and every held-out step is green.

- [ ] A run over two independent tickets builds both and leaves two merge commits on the main line.

- [ ] A stuck ticket blocks its dependents only; an unrelated ticket still merges.
- [ ] A stopped loop leaves no ticket in building or merging.
- [ ] A main line moved by someone else during the merge checks is not overwritten.
- [ ] A run started on a child of a subtree with a run in progress is refused and names that run.

- `make lint`

blocked_by: 35
stories: 93, 94
touches: merge loop, build scheduler, merge queue

## What to build

The merge loop builds up to three ready tickets at the same time, each in its own worktree branched from the main line's tip when its build starts. It starts a ticket next to the running ones only when the names on its touches line share none with theirs, comparing names only; a ticket that shares a module waits until the other has merged. The merge queue still takes one ticket at a time.

When git cannot merge a ticket, its next pass starts from its own branch with the main line's tip merged in; the builder gets the conflicted files and the conflict output. That pass does not count against the retry cap. A ticket that comes back green from a conflict pass goes to the front of the merge queue. Three conflicts in a row mark it stuck.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Three tickets with disjoint touches build at once; a fourth waits.
- [ ] Two tickets sharing one touches name never build at the same time.
- [ ] A ticket whose branch conflicts with an earlier merge gets a conflict pass from its own branch and its pass count does not rise.
- [ ] After a green conflict pass that ticket merges before any other waiting ticket.
- [ ] A third conflict in a row marks the ticket stuck.

After each merge the held-out set starts on that merge's commit in the background, with the steps of every merged ticket of the subtree including the one just merged; steps of tickets still building, merging or archived stay out. - [ ] A step that is red again while its follow-up is open files nothing.

`/board` shows the project's board from the board fold: columns blocked, ready, building, merging and done, each at least 200 pixels wide, sharing extra width, with a sideways scrollbar on a narrow screen. For a building ticket, a fixed-height live preview above the slice shows one summarised line per event of its session file, overseer lines included, each with its full time; it goes when the ticket leaves building. A line above the columns shows G2 per subtree, waiting or passed. The board redraws on the live channel.

- [ ] A fixture board log shows each ticket in its column.

- [ ] A cited card id in the sidebar opens that card on the map.
- [ ] The Decisions section shows a proposed card, and "No new card" with the followed cards for a build that recorded them.
- [ ] At a narrow width the board scrolls sideways and columns keep their width.

title: A person reorders ready tickets, triggers one early inside a run, and archives a ticket with a confirmation that ends its build
cites: werk-board-control
blocked_by: 36, 38
stories: 69, 70
touches: board controls, ticket drawer, board write routes, builder loop

## What to build

On the board a person drags tickets within ready to reorder them, and the run builds them in that order. Inside an active run, the trigger icon on a ready ticket, or a drag from ready into building, starts that ticket's build early; it joins the run's merge loop, which still builds at most three at once. The drag into building is the only manual column move. Without an active run, the trigger is disabled.

Archive is a button in the drawer header of a ready, blocked or building ticket, never of a merging or done one. It asks for confirmation and says the ticket is never deleted for good and can be restored. Archiving a building ticket ends its build: the builder loop reads the board about once a second, and when it finds its ticket archived it stops the agent, commits nothing of the pass, runs no checks, records no retry, removes the worktree folder and keeps the branch. Nothing of that build merges, even a green last pass; the merge loop goes on with its other tickets. Cancelling the confirmation writes nothing. An archived ticket shows a restore action that puts it back in the column it left. Every action is a write with the token.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Reordering ready tickets changes the order in which the run builds them.
- [ ] The trigger on a ready ticket inside a run starts its build; outside a run it is disabled.
- [ ] Archiving a building ticket stops its agent within about a second and its branch remains.
- [ ] Other tickets of the same run keep building after an archive.
- [ ] Cancelling the archive confirmation leaves the board log unchanged.
- [ ] A merging or done ticket shows no archive button.
- [ ] Restoring an archived ticket from the board returns it to its old column with its old reason.

## Checks

- `make test`
- `make typecheck`
- `make lint`
- `make e2e`

title: One Build press on a decided card plans its subtree and runs it as one detached process, shown on a plan card that can resume or restart it
cites:
blocked_by: 39, 77
stories: 71, 72, 73
touches: plan card, build button, run starter, board view, card page

## What to build

A decided map card carries a Build button. It works only when the plan's scope holds no open or proto card; otherwise it is grey and names the blocking cards. A press starts one detached process with no time limit that plans the subtree and then runs the merge loop; it outlives a server restart.

Below the columns, each planned subtree has one persistent plan card, at most four lines high, linked to its subtree on the map and from each of its tickets. It is coloured by state: creating (pulsing, naming the running step), building, done, or stopped with its reason; a plan whose process is gone without an end shows stopped. Its drawer shows both writers' logs from their session files, then the whole spec, its tickets and how the last plan ended. While a plan runs, the subtree root on the map carries a marker linking to the plan card.

A subtree with unfinished work (a ticket in ready, blocked, building or merging) offers Resume, which restarts the merge loop, and a confirmed Restart, which cancels running builds keeping their branches, archives every unfinished ticket, keeps done ones, and plans and runs again. The map card and the plan card show the same control for the same state, and the map card never shows an enabled Build while unfinished work exists. Every start of a plan or run, from the board or the command line, refuses while a run is in progress on the subtree or an ancestor and names the blocking run; disabled controls stay visible, say so and link to its plan card. The command-line restart prints each build it cancels and each ticket it archives and needs a confirmation flag.

## Acceptance criteria

## What to build

A build runs in its own process, apart from the server, so it can die alone: a kill, a crash, a machine sleep. The server watches for a dead build at two moments: when a build process it started exits, and when the server itself starts. A build is dead when the board log has a start for it, no end, and its named process is gone. A build whose process is alive is left alone, whichever server started it.

For each dead build the server writes its end with the reason died, then starts a fresh pass of the same ticket from the last commit on the ticket's branch, with the death as the last failure in the brief. The fresh pass counts against the ticket's retry cap, so a build that dies on every pass stops at the cap with died as the reason. Work the dead pass did not commit is lost. The death is a step end in the pipeline log too.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A build process killed while the server runs gets a died end and a fresh pass starts from the branch's last commit.
- [ ] A build killed while the server is down gets its died end and fresh pass when the server starts.
- [ ] The fresh pass's prompt says the last pass died.
- [ ] A build that dies on its last allowed pass stops with died as the reason and no new pass starts.
- [ ] A live build started by an earlier server is not touched.

## Checks

- `make test`

- `make lint`
